evidence_fragments.source_ref: Papers/088_2025_PRIME-Care A Unified Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Optimization Framework for Personalized Treatment Planning Under Clinical Uncertaint.pdf
evidence_fragments.content:
The PRIME-Care experiments relied on two complementary data sourc es. The ﬁrst
dataset consisted of longitudinal, de-identiﬁed electronic health r ecords (EHR) from a
regional multicenter chronic-care program, comprising approximately 19,000 patient
trajectories with irregular time sampling and heterogeneous covariat es. The dataset
included demographic attributes, laboratory results, clinician-re corded disease severity
indices, administered interventions, and adverse-event marker s. Because PRIME-Care
explicitly models uncertainty propagation, the irregularity and incompleteness
of the trajectories provided a realistic testbed for evaluating th e eﬀectiveness of the
framework’s probabilistic state estimators, which were designed to handle missingness
without information leakage.
The second data source consisted of high-ﬁdelity digital-twin simul ation environ-
ments parameterized by the real clinical data distribution. These simulators were
developed using physiologically meaningful nonlinear dynamics relate d to chronic dis-
ease progression and were validated through expert-driven calibration p rocedures.

evidence_fragments.source_ref: Papers/088_2025_PRIME-Care A Unified Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Optimization Framework for Personalized Treatment Planning Under Clinical Uncertaint.pdf
evidence_fragments.content:
All experiments were conducted under a sequential decision-maki ng setting in
which PRIME-Care determined individualized intervention seq uences such as med-
ication titration, scheduling of diagnostic assessments, and lifesty le adjustment
recommendations. A clinical advisory board oversaw the mapping betwe en algorithm
outputs and clinically feasible actions, ensuring that the simulati on does not include
unrealistic therapeutic choices.

evidence_fragments.source_ref: Papers/088_2025_PRIME-Care A Unified Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Optimization Framework for Personalized Treatment Planning Under Clinical Uncertaint.pdf
evidence_fragments.content:
Each baseline was executed using identical patient histories, cov ariate representa-
tions, and digital-twin dynamics. Hyperparameters and training sched ules were tuned
through systematic cross-validation to prevent confounding performan ce diﬀerences
due to suboptimal conﬁgurations. This comparative setup allowed for an un biased
assessment of the hybrid RL optimization structure in PRIME-Care, isolating con-
tributions from constraint feasibility modeling, belief-state un certainty handling, and
the bilevel decision structure.
6.3 Evaluation Metrics
The evaluation protocol was designed to assess four principal dimension s of algorithmic
and clinical performance: patient safety, personalization ﬁdelity, p redictive accuracy,
and robustness under perturbation. Safety was quantiﬁed through the f requency of
constraint violations involving medically deﬁned thresholds for adve rse biomarkers or
treatment toxicity. Personalization quality was assessed via traje ctory similarity analy-
sis, measuring the alignment between algorithm-generated plans and ex pert-annotated
individualized strategies. Predictive accuracy was evaluated usin g the negative log-
likelihood of state-transition predictions and the concordance inde x for longitudinal
progression forecasting.
Robustness was measured by evaluating the stability of treatment dec isions under
perturbations to model parameters, missingness patterns, and stoc hastic noise within
the digital twin. PRIME-Care’s probabilistic formulation permitte d uncertainty-aware
variants of these metrics, enabling direct comparisons with uncert ainty-agnostic RL
baselines. All metrics were reported with conﬁdence intervals de rived from 5,000
bootstrap resamples to ensure statistical reliability.

All models were trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU with batch size 64. Hyper-
parameters were tuned using Bayesian optimization. For fairness, su bgroup analyses
included sex, age ( <60 vs. ≥60), and comorbidity index.
Cross-validation was performed using 5-fold CV; performance metrics we re
reported on the independent held-out test set only .
7.3 Results and Analysis
This subsection follows TRIPOD+AI’s required structure: (i) m odel performance, (ii)
calibration, (iii) robustness, (iv) fairness, (v) interpretabil ity, (vi) clinical utility, and
(vii) failure analysis. Quantitative and qualitative ﬁndings are repor ted to maximize
transparency.
